name: How the CNI and CoreDNS work
objective: CKA › Services & Networking + Troubleshooting. Drill the whole pod-networking surface harder than the exam: how the CNI hands out pod IPs from the pod CIDR, the node-level CNI config, a no-hint diagnose-and-fix for a broken CNI, CoreDNS resolution, ClusterIP + endpoints, the full pod→Service datapath, headless Services, and NodePort. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: The CNI hands out pod IPs from the pod CIDR
questions.teach:
Kubernetes doesn't wire pod networking itself — a **CNI plugin** does. The kubelet calls it to attach each pod and lease it an IP out of the cluster **pod CIDR** (here `10.244.0.0/16`). See it with `kubectl get pod -o wide`.

**Gotcha:** no / broken CNI means no IP, so the pod is stuck `Pending`/`ContainerCreating` — never `Running`.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `cni-learn`, run a pod named `netcheck` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`).

Target: `netcheck` is `Running` with a `.status.podIP` inside the pod CIDR `10.244.0.0/16`.
questions.hint: `kubectl run netcheck -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600`, then `kubectl get pod netcheck -n cni-learn -o wide` — the IP should start with `10.244.`.
questions.solution:
kubectl run netcheck -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl get pod netcheck -n cni-learn -o wide

verification.description: netcheck is Running with a pod-CIDR IP (10.244.0.0/16)

questions.eli5:
Kubernetes itself is strangely hands-off about networking. It knows how to start your container, but it does **not** know how to give it an IP address or plug it into the network. It delegates that entirely to a helper called a **CNI plugin** (Container Network Interface).

Think of it like moving into an apartment building. The building manager (Kubernetes/kubelet) assigns you a unit and unlocks the door, but a separate **utility company (the CNI)** is the one that actually runs the wiring and gives your unit its own address. No utility company hooked up = you have a room but no address and no phone line.

The addresses all come from one big block the cluster owns, called the **pod CIDR** — here `10.244.0.0/16`. Every pod gets a unique IP out of that block. When your `netcheck` pod starts, the kubelet calls the CNI, the CNI leases it an IP like `10.244.1.7`, and the pod goes `Running`. You can see the IP with `kubectl get pod -o wide`.

**Watch out for:**

- **No CNI (or a broken one) = no IP = no Running pod.** The pod gets stuck in `Pending` or, more often, `ContainerCreating` — it can never reach `Running` without an address. This is a super-common exam/real-world failure.
- The pod IP comes from the **pod CIDR** (`10.244.x.x` here), which is totally different from Service IPs (the `10.96.x.x` service CIDR) and from node IPs. Don't confuse the three.
- Pod IPs are **ephemeral** — delete and recreate the pod and it usually gets a different IP. Never hardcode a pod IP; use a Service.
- `-o wide` is what reveals the IP and node; plain `kubectl get pod` hides it.
questions.deepDive:
## The CNI & pod IPs — full rundown

### The one-sentence model
Kubernetes does **not** implement pod networking. The **kubelet calls a CNI plugin** (via the Container Network Interface spec) for every pod; the plugin creates the pod's network interface and **leases it an IP from the cluster pod CIDR**. No CNI → no IP → the pod never reaches `Running`.

### The three IP ranges (do not confuse them)
| Range | Example here | Who lives there | Set by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pod CIDR** | `10.244.0.0/16` | every pod IP | CNI / `--cluster-cidr` / `--pod-network-cidr` |
| **Service CIDR** | `10.96.0.0/12` | clusterIPs of Services | apiserver `--service-cluster-ip-range` |
| **Node IPs** | e.g. `172.18.0.x` (kind) | the nodes themselves | infra / network |

Each **node** gets a non-overlapping slice of the pod CIDR in `.spec.podCIDR` (e.g. `10.244.1.0/24`), and the CNI hands IPs out of that node's slice to pods on that node.

### Seeing it
```bash
kubectl run netcheck -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl get pod netcheck -n cni-learn -o wide     # IP column shows 10.244.x.y, plus NODE
kubectl get pod netcheck -n cni-learn -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}'; echo

# the per-node slices
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,CIDR:.spec.podCIDR
```

### How attachment works (lifecycle)
1. Scheduler assigns the pod to a node.
2. kubelet creates the pod sandbox (pause container) via the CRI.
3. kubelet invokes the CNI `ADD` operation (reads config from `/etc/cni/net.d/`).
4. CNI creates a veth pair, moves one end into the pod netns, assigns an IP from the node's pod-CIDR slice, programs routes.
5. `status.podIP` is populated; the pod can go `Running`.
On delete, kubelet calls CNI `DEL` to release the IP and tear down the interface.

### Common CNI plugins
| Plugin | Model | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **kindnet** | simple host routing | default in `kind` clusters |
| **Calico** | BGP / routing, NetworkPolicy | very common in CKA material |
| **Flannel** | VXLAN overlay | simple overlay |
| **Cilium** | eBPF | NetworkPolicy + observability |
| **Weave** | overlay | legacy |

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **No/broken CNI → pod stuck `ContainerCreating` or `Pending`, never `Running`.** `kubectl describe pod` shows `NetworkPluginNotReady` / `cni config uninitialized`.
- The **pod IP ≠ Service clusterIP ≠ node IP** — know which range is which (`10.244.*` pod vs `10.96.*` service here).
- **Pod IPs are ephemeral**: recreating a pod usually changes its IP. Address pods via Services/DNS, never a hardcoded IP.
- `kubectl get pod` hides the IP — use **`-o wide`** or jsonpath.
- CNI runs as a **DaemonSet** (here kindnet) so every node has the plugin; if the DaemonSet pod is missing on a node, that node can't network new pods.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl run netcheck -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl get pod netcheck -n cni-learn -o wide         # IP starts 10.244.
kubectl get pod netcheck -n cni-learn \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}'; echo
```

questions.title: The CNI config lives on the node
questions.teach:
Each node carries its CNI config under `/etc/cni/net.d/`; the kubelet reads the first `*.conflist` there to know which plugin to call. On a kind node that file is `10-kindnet.conflist`, written by the kindnet DaemonSet. Each node also owns a slice of the pod CIDR in `.spec.podCIDR`.

**Gotcha:** the kubelet picks files in lexical order — a stray `00-*.conf` would shadow the real one.
questions.prompt:
No cluster change is needed here — this step inspects node `$W1`. It passes once node `$W1` has a `.spec.podCIDR` inside `10.244.0.0/16` AND the file `/etc/cni/net.d/10-kindnet.conflist` exists on that node.

Target: `$W1` has a podCIDR and its kindnet CNI conflist is present.
questions.hint: `kubectl get node $W1 -o jsonpath='{.spec.podCIDR}'` shows the node's slice; `docker exec $W1 ls /etc/cni/net.d` lists the CNI config. Both already hold on a healthy node.
questions.solution:
kubectl get node $W1 -o jsonpath='{.spec.podCIDR}'; echo
docker exec $W1 ls -l /etc/cni/net.d/10-kindnet.conflist

verification.description: $W1 has a podCIDR in 10.244.0.0/16 and /etc/cni/net.d/10-kindnet.conflist exists on the node

questions.eli5:
Every node needs to know *which* networking utility company to call and how to reach it. That instruction sheet lives as a file **on the node itself**, in the folder `/etc/cni/net.d/`.

Think of it like a **pinned sticky note by the phone**: "To hook up a new tenant, call this company, using these settings." When the kubelet needs to wire up a new pod, it walks over to that folder, reads the instruction file, and follows it. On a kind cluster the file is `10-kindnet.conflist`, and it's written there by the **kindnet DaemonSet** (the pod that runs the networking on every node).

There's also a second piece: each node is handed its own **slice of the big address block** — stored as `.spec.podCIDR` on the node object (e.g. node1 owns `10.244.1.0/24`). So the node knows both *who* to call (the conflist) and *what addresses* it's allowed to hand out (its podCIDR slice).

The folder can hold several files, and here's the sneaky part: the kubelet reads them in **alphabetical order and uses the first valid one**. So the filename prefix (the `10-`) is actually a priority.

**Watch out for:**

- **Lexical (alphabetical) ordering matters.** A stray file like `00-something.conf` sorts *before* `10-kindnet.conflist` and would **shadow** the real config — the kubelet would use the wrong one. Leftover or misnamed files are a classic trap.
- This config lives **on the node's filesystem**, not in the Kubernetes API. You inspect it with `docker exec <node> ls /etc/cni/net.d`, not `kubectl`.
- `.conf` vs `.conflist`: a `.conflist` chains multiple plugins; both are read, but naming/precedence still follows lexical order.
- If this file goes missing, the node can't network new pods at all — that's the exact failure the "nodefix" lab makes you repair.
questions.deepDive:
## Node-level CNI config & podCIDR — full rundown

### The one-sentence model
Each node tells the kubelet which CNI plugin to call via a config file in **`/etc/cni/net.d/`**; the kubelet uses the **first valid file in lexical order**. The node's share of the pod address space is stored in the node object's **`.spec.podCIDR`**.

### Where the pieces live
| Piece | Location | Inspect with |
|---|---|---|
| CNI config | `/etc/cni/net.d/*.conf` / `*.conflist` (on the node) | `docker exec <node> ls /etc/cni/net.d` |
| CNI binaries | `/opt/cni/bin/` (on the node) | `docker exec <node> ls /opt/cni/bin` |
| Node's pod-CIDR slice | `.spec.podCIDR` (API object) | `kubectl get node <n> -o jsonpath='{.spec.podCIDR}'` |

In `kind`, nodes are Docker containers, so you reach the node filesystem with `docker exec <node> …`, not `kubectl`.

### The config file
```bash
docker exec $W1 ls -l /etc/cni/net.d
# 10-kindnet.conflist
docker exec $W1 cat /etc/cni/net.d/10-kindnet.conflist
```
- `.conf` = a single plugin config.
- `.conflist` = an ordered **chain** of plugins (e.g. main plugin + portmap + bandwidth) under a `plugins: []` array.
- The numeric prefix (`10-`) sets **precedence by filename sort**.

### File selection order (the trap)
The kubelet (via the CNI runtime) scans `/etc/cni/net.d/` and picks the **lexically first** valid config:
```
00-anything.conf      ← chosen first (sorts earliest)
10-kindnet.conflist   ← the real one, shadowed if a 00-* exists
99-loopback.conf
```
A stray `00-*.conf` would override the intended plugin — a classic "why is networking broken" cause.

### podCIDR: cluster vs node
```bash
# cluster-wide pod CIDR (controller-manager flag)
#   --cluster-cidr=10.244.0.0/16   (set at cluster bootstrap)

# per-node slice carved from it
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,CIDR:.spec.podCIDR
# kindlab-worker   10.244.1.0/24
# kindlab-worker2  10.244.2.0/24
```
The kube-controller-manager's **IPAM** (when `--allocate-node-cidrs=true`) assigns each node a non-overlapping `/24` (by default) from the cluster CIDR; the CNI then leases pod IPs from that node's slice.

### Verifying a healthy node
```bash
kubectl get node $W1 -o jsonpath='{.spec.podCIDR}'; echo   # e.g. 10.244.1.0/24
docker exec $W1 ls -l /etc/cni/net.d/10-kindnet.conflist   # file present
```
Both must hold: a podCIDR inside `10.244.0.0/16` **and** the kindnet conflist present.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Lexical ordering**: a `00-*.conf` shadows the intended config. Clean up stray/leftover files.
- CNI config is **on the node filesystem**, not in the API — use `docker exec`/node shell, not `kubectl`.
- **Missing conflist** → `cni config uninitialized` / `NetworkPluginNotReady`; new pods stick in `ContainerCreating`.
- CNI **binaries** (`/opt/cni/bin`) are separate from config — a config referencing a missing binary also fails.
- The kindnet DaemonSet **rewrites `10-kindnet.conflist` on pod start**, so restarting its pod on a node restores a deleted config (see the nodefix lab).
- `.spec.podCIDR` missing on a node → the CNI has no range to allocate from; check controller-manager `--allocate-node-cidrs`/`--cluster-cidr`.

### Quick reference
```bash
docker exec $W1 ls /etc/cni/net.d                          # 10-kindnet.conflist
docker exec $W1 ls /opt/cni/bin                            # plugin binaries
kubectl get node $W1 -o jsonpath='{.spec.podCIDR}'; echo   # 10.244.x.0/24
```

questions.title: CoreDNS resolves Service names
questions.teach:
**CoreDNS** answers in-cluster DNS, resolving a Service's FQDN `<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local` to its clusterIP. Test from a pod with `nslookup <fqdn>`; a resolved `Address:` line means DNS works.

**Gotcha:** busybox `nslookup` is flaky with the `search` list — always query the **full FQDN**, not a short name, for a deterministic answer.
questions.prompt:
Run a pod named `dnscheck` (image `busybox:1.36`, `--restart=Never`) that resolves the API Service by its FQDN `kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local`.

Target: `dnscheck`'s logs show a resolved `Address` for that FQDN (no NXDOMAIN / 'can't resolve').
questions.hint: `kubectl run dnscheck -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never --command -- nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local`, then `kubectl logs dnscheck -n cni-learn`.
questions.solution:
kubectl run dnscheck -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never --command -- nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
kubectl logs dnscheck -n cni-learn   # Address: 10.96.0.1
questions.eli5:
Pods talk to each other by **name**, not by memorizing ever-changing IP addresses. The thing that turns a name into an address is **CoreDNS** — the cluster's own little phone book, running as pods inside the cluster.

When a pod asks "what's the address of `web`?", CoreDNS looks it up and answers with that Service's IP. Every Service automatically gets a full, official name shaped like:

`<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`

So the Kubernetes API Service is `kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local` — service `kubernetes`, in namespace `default`. Ask CoreDNS for that name and it answers with `10.96.0.1` (the API's clusterIP). You test it from inside a pod with `nslookup <name>`; seeing an `Address:` line back means DNS is working.

Every pod is pre-configured to use CoreDNS automatically — Kubernetes writes the DNS server and a list of **search suffixes** into each pod's `/etc/resolv.conf`, so short names like `web` can be auto-completed to the full name.

**Watch out for:**

- **busybox `nslookup` is flaky with short names.** The search-suffix auto-completion can misbehave in busybox, giving confusing or wrong answers. Always query the **full FQDN** (`kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local`) for a deterministic result.
- A `can't resolve` / `NXDOMAIN` reply means DNS failed — usually CoreDNS is down, or you used a name that doesn't exist.
- The FQDN pieces matter: a Service in namespace `foo` is `<svc>.foo.svc.cluster.local`, **not** `.default.`. Wrong namespace = wrong (or no) answer.
- Pods (not Services) have DNS too, but their names use dashes-for-dots and the `.pod.` segment — different format; don't mix them up.
- `--restart=Never` makes this a one-shot pod; its `nslookup` output lands in the pod logs.
questions.deepDive:
## CoreDNS & cluster DNS — full rundown

### The one-sentence model
**CoreDNS** is the in-cluster DNS server (pods in `kube-system`, fronted by the `kube-dns` Service). It resolves a Service's FQDN **`<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local`** to its clusterIP, and gives pods name-based discovery. Every pod's `/etc/resolv.conf` points at it.

### DNS name formats
| Object | DNS name | Resolves to |
|---|---|---|
| Service (normal) | `<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local` | the clusterIP (1 A record) |
| Service (headless) | `<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local` | each pod IP (N A records) |
| StatefulSet pod | `<pod>.<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local` | that pod's IP |
| Pod (by IP) | `<ip-with-dashes>.<ns>.pod.cluster.local` | the pod IP |
| SRV (ports) | `_<port>._<proto>.<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local` | port + target |

Examples:
```
kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local   → 10.96.0.1   (the API Service)
web.cni-learn.svc.cluster.local        → the web clusterIP
10-244-1-5.cni-learn.pod.cluster.local → 10.244.1.5
```

### resolv.conf inside a pod
```bash
kubectl exec dnscheck -n cni-learn -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
# nameserver 10.96.0.10                         # kube-dns Service clusterIP
# search cni-learn.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
# options ndots:5
```
- `nameserver` = the `kube-dns` Service clusterIP (CoreDNS behind it).
- `search` = suffixes tried for short names (own namespace first).
- **`ndots:5`** = names with fewer than 5 dots get the search suffixes appended before being tried as absolute — why `web` and `web.cni-learn` resolve.

### Testing resolution
```bash
kubectl run dnscheck -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never \
  --command -- nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
kubectl logs dnscheck -n cni-learn        # expect an Address: line (10.96.0.1)

# interactive, cleans up after:
kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never \
  -- nslookup web.cni-learn.svc.cluster.local
```

### Inspecting CoreDNS itself
```bash
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns       # CoreDNS pods
kubectl get svc  -n kube-system kube-dns                  # usually 10.96.0.10
kubectl -n kube-system get configmap coredns -o yaml      # the Corefile
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns           # query/errors
```
A typical Corefile uses the `kubernetes` plugin for `cluster.local` + reverse zones, `forward . /etc/resolv.conf` for upstream, and `cache`.

### DNS policy (on the pod)
| `dnsPolicy` | Effect |
|---|---|
| `ClusterFirst` (default) | cluster DNS first, then upstream |
| `Default` | inherit the node's resolv.conf |
| `None` | fully custom via `dnsConfig` |
| `ClusterFirstWithHostNet` | cluster DNS even with `hostNetwork: true` |

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **busybox `nslookup` + search list is unreliable** → always query the **FQDN** for deterministic results.
- **Wrong namespace in the name**: a Service in `foo` is `<svc>.foo.svc.cluster.local`, not `.default.`.
- `NXDOMAIN` / `can't resolve` → CoreDNS down, bad name, or `kube-dns` Service/endpoints missing. Check CoreDNS pods and logs.
- Pod DNS names use **dashes for dots** and the `.pod.` segment — different from Service names.
- `hostNetwork: true` pods need `dnsPolicy: ClusterFirstWithHostNet` to use cluster DNS.
- The DNS nameserver is the **`kube-dns` Service clusterIP** (commonly `10.96.0.10`), not a CoreDNS pod IP.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl run dnscheck -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never \
  --command -- nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
kubectl logs dnscheck -n cni-learn        # Address: 10.96.0.1
# svc FQDN: <svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local
```
